name: Lough Gur
summary: The enchanted lake of the south-west: Innis Carthaig and Culraid, the doors into the hills, the weeping queen, the headless riders and the lord of the mice.

facts.text: Lough Gur in County Limerick is rich in legend: the Earl Gearóid Iarla is said to sleep beneath it and ride out every seventh year, and the lake is linked with the goddess Áine.
In Irish folklore the dullahan is a headless rider whose coming foretells a death; the fear liath ('grey man') is the fog that brings travellers to grief.
In the medieval tale of Seanchán Torpéist the poet satirises the mice that ate his dinner, and then the cats, and Irusan, king of cats, comes to carry him off.
Luchtigern read as 'mouse-lord' (luch, mouse; tigern, lord): to verify.

Living Server lore: the lake of doors; the court under the water and the queen shut out of it; the trumpets; the headless riders' road; the gurite; Luchtigern's hall; the rats of Innis Carthaig and the piper; Brac's book.

Tier C named spawns of Lough Gur: Luchtigern (32, a rat body, DOL.GS.DaySpawn: shown only by day), Trefor (29, gurite; Occupation of Lough Gur; aggressive though the quest speaks to him), Brannigan (28, leprechaun; respawn 600 s).

The Horn Twin (Harmony50.cs): Revelin, a peaceful level-20 NPC the script creates at 343,442/706,235 in region 200 if none exists, sends Blademasters, Druids, Valewalkers, Animists and Mentalists to 'Seek out Cailean in Cursed Forest and kill it'; the horn is given to Revelin for the epic armour.

story:
Lough Gur is ringed with doors. The hills around the lake are hollow, the people of Innis Carthaig say, and the doors into them are everywhere, in the faces of rocks and under old trees and at the bottoms of pools, and most of them have been shut since the Veil came down. On summer nights there is music under the water, trumpets and harps, the court of the lake keeping its feasts, and every grandmother of the realm says the same thing about it: if the trumpets sound after dark, go home.

Two women of the lake have been shut out. The Melancholic Fairy Queen sits by a door in the hills of the south-west that will not open for her; she was shut out of her own kingdom on the night the courts quarrelled in the Cursed Forest, the Ardee folk say, and she comes to the door every night with her guard behind her, to a fanfare from no instrument anyone can find, and weeps by the water until morning. The melancholic fairies of her court weep with her in the hills, and the militant ones stand over them. Lhia was of the court under the water until Piaras of Howth broke the condition she set him, a year and a day and never by daylight, and the court shut its door on her. She walks the shore looking for him, and takes everyone for him at first.

There are worse things on the lake roads. The dullahans ride the middle shore, headless, and the old people of Innis Carthaig say that a dullahan stopping at a house means a death in it before the month is out. The far liath comes off the western hills as fog and leads walkers into the water. The scanradh, whose name is only the word for fright, wait in the high ground of the south-west. And the gurite, the siabra of the lake country, hold camps all round the shore, waylayers and footpads and ambushers who rob the lake roads and lookouts who watch them.

The lake has a lord of the mice. Luchtigern keeps a hall in the west of the lake country among the irewoods, and the luch, the great mice of Lough Gur, large and greater, are his, and the luch catchers and hunters who track them are trying to get to him. The bards of Innis Carthaig sing an old satire in which a poet mocked the king of cats and the mice laughed, and say Luchtigern is the mouse who laughed loudest. The rats are another matter. Rats came into Innis Carthaig and stole the staff the smith Glennard made for the chieftess, and carried it to their den on the hillside, and the town has been paying pipers ever since.

Innis Carthaig is the lake's chief town, on its eastern shore, where Chieftess Niamh keeps her hall and Sholto and Kern the enchanter keep the lake's errands, and the realm's companies stop on their way to Shannon or the bog. Culraid stands in the north-west, smaller and older, under Chief Bran Llyr, whose townsfolk have gone missing into the lake country and who sends the realm after them. In the west the irewoods grow thick, and beyond them is the entrance to Treibh Caillte, where King Vian's lost tribe keep their halls. Old Donnchadh keeps a camp in the east hills with a nightshade commander, and knows about the beast the Last Heir hunts.

Why does it matter? Because Lough Gur is where the realm keeps its manners with the Otherworld. The druids of Lough Gur, the oldest in the realm, were taught at this lake, Brónach among them; they say that every door around it is a promise one side or the other made and has not kept, and that the lake is the nearest the realm comes to the courts' own country. The trumpets sound most nights. The realm goes home.
legend: Lough Gur is the south-west lake zone, levels 22-56. Innis Carthaig (east shore) is the town: channeler, merchants, Chieftess Niamh, Sholto and Kern for Morven's Return and Occupation of Lough Gur. Culraid (north-west) has Chief Bran Llyr. The Treibh Caillte entrance is in the west. Camps: irewood saplings (22-37) in the west, large luch (32-37) and dampwood mites by Innis Carthaig, giant ants, the gurite siabra camps all round the lake (30-49, social), melancholic fairies (45-50) in the south-west hills, dullahans and pookas (49-56) on the middle shore, deamhans in the south. The Melancholic Fairy Queen (65) comes at night with trumpets and five guards; Lhia (53) is the last kill of Piaras and Lhia. Lots of tier B named (Smidget, Smirky, Curmie, Tiomoid, Ailbe). Superstition: if you hear trumpets after dark, go home, and never answer a dullahan at your door.

loremaster.intro: Lough Gur, the lake of [doors]. Two women are shut out: the [queen] and [Lhia]. The [dullahans] ride, the [gurite] rob, and the [mice] have a lord. [Innis Carthaig] and [Culraid] keep the shore. Mind the [trumpets].

topics.doors: The doors into the hollow hills around the lake, in rocks and under trees and at the bottoms of pools, shut since the Veil came down. The Lough Gur druids say every one is a promise somebody did not keep.
topics.queen: The Melancholic Fairy Queen, shut out of her kingdom the night the courts quarrelled. She weeps by her door in the south-west hills every night with her guard. Strangers who come instead of her people are not welcome.
topics.Lhia: Of the court under the water, until Piaras of Howth came to see her by daylight on the last day of the year and a day. The court shut its door on her. She walks the shore and takes everyone for him at first.
topics.dullahans: Headless riders of the middle shore. A dullahan stopping at a house means a death in it before the month is out, the old people say. Nobody answers the door to one.
topics.gurite: The siabra of the lake country: waylayers, footpads, ambushers, raiders and lookouts in camps all round the lake, robbing the lake roads. Tiomoid of the siabra is among them.
topics.mice: The luch, the great mice of Lough Gur, and their lord Luchtigern in his hall among the western irewoods. The bards say he is the mouse who laughed loudest in the old satire on the king of cats.
topics.Innis Carthaig: The lake's chief town on the eastern shore: Chieftess Niamh's hall, Sholto and Kern, Harper Brac, and rats. The rats stole the chieftess's staff; the town pays pipers.
topics.Culraid: The small old town in the north-west under Chief Bran Llyr, whose townsfolk keep going missing into the lake country, and the cluricauns Smidget and Smirky who will not leave his fields.
topics.trumpets: The music of the court under the water, which sounds on summer nights. Every grandmother of the realm says the same thing: if the trumpets sound after dark, go home. The queen comes to them.
topics.Luchtigern: Luchtigern is the lord of the luch, the great mice of Lough Gur, and he keeps his hall among the western irewoods. The bards of Innis Carthaig sing an old satire in which a poet mocked the king of cats and the mice laughed, and they say Luchtigern is the mouse who laughed loudest. He keeps court by daylight and not after, as mice do not, and the luch catchers who hunt his people come to his hall in the morning, and find it empty by night.
topics.Trefor: Trefor is the gurite of the raider camp in the south-west who deals with the realm, or seems to. Aziliz of Lough Derg sends the young to find out what the gurite siabra are doing at the lake, and the road leads to Trefor, who takes a bundle of daggers and a ring and talks about treasure hunting, and asks for more. Harper Brac thinks the gurite are digging for something under the lake. Trefor thinks it is funny that anyone asks.
topics.Brannigan: Brannigan is a leprechaun of the southern shore, big for one, who claims to have been at the court under the water when the doors shut and to have got out by the last of them. Nobody believes him, and he does not need them to. He keeps to himself in the hills above the shore, and the dullahans of the riders' road go round his ground, which is more than they do for anyone else.
topics.Revelin: Revelin keeps company with old Donnchadh at his camp on the east of the lake, and is the one the realm's champions of the green paths come to when they are ready, the blademasters and druids, the valewalkers, animists and mentalists. Revelin sends them to the Cursed Forest after Cailean, a tree gone mad with terror, north-west of the grannies' fort across the river, and asks them to bring back its horn. The horn has a twin, Revelin says, and will not say where.

book.title: The Lake of Doors, by Harper Brac of Innis Carthaig
pages: A harper of Innis Carthaig learns two kinds of music: the kind he plays and the kind he listens for. The second kind comes from under the lake on summer nights, trumpets and harps, a court at its feast behind a door. My master taught me to listen to it from the shore and never to answer it with my own harp, because a door that hears its own music played back to it opens, and nobody on this side knows what comes out. I have kept that rule forty years. My harp is very quiet in summer.

Two women of the lake were shut out of it, and both of them still come to the shore. The queen of the south-west came with her guard the night the courts quarrelled in the forest and found her own door shut, and she has wept by it every night since. The other was Lhia, of the court under the water, who promised herself to Piaras of Howth on the old condition and lost him to an afternoon. The court shut its door on her too. She walks the shore. When she looks up at a footstep, I keep walking.

The roads have their own dangers. The headless riders come along the middle shore at night, and when one stops at a house there is a death in that house before the month is out; I have seen it twice. The grey man comes off the western hills as fog. The siabra of the lake rob the roads, and the town's guard is only so large. And there are the mice, great ones, and their lord in his hall in the irewoods, of whom we sing the old satire, very quietly, because he can hear it.

Innis Carthaig has rats as well. They took the chieftess's staff from Glennard's forge and carried it up the hillside to their den, and we paid a piper to bring it back, and now we pay one every season, because the rats have learned that we will. The chieftess says it is cheaper than the alternative. I play at her hall in the evenings and listen, under my own tune, for the other music. When I hear it, I stop, and we all go home, and nobody asks me to finish the tune.
